msg: Paper 89 deals with how the concepts of sin, sacrifice, and atonement evolved. Primitive people believed the gods were pleased to see human suffering, so they kept taboos, practiced austerities, and offered sacrifices. Today's passage shows one stage of that evolution. The idea of making a covenant with the gods did finally arrive, and evolutionary man eventually acquired such moral dignity that he dared to bargain with his gods. But the business of offering sacrifices gradually developed into the game of man's philosophic bargaining with God, an enhanced technique for insuring against bad luck and for the more definite purchase of prosperity.

The passage warns plainly: do not entertain the mistaken idea that these early sacrifices were a free gift to the gods, a spontaneous offering of gratitude or thanksgiving; they were not expressions of true worship. Primitive offerings were not gifts of love but payments in a transaction. Underneath lay the calculation that whatever was offered would return as an equal reward. God was a partner in bargaining, and religion was insurance against loss. In it there was neither gratitude nor love, only fear and calculation.

But is this really a story of bygone ages? Even today many people bargain with God. They expect that giving generously will make their business prosper, believe that serving diligently will heal their illness, and think that praying long will get them what they want. Beneath this attitude lies the idea that God's favor can be bought with something. But The Urantia Book teaches that God's love can never be purchased; it is already given freely.

The religion of bargaining and the religion of worship start from different places. The religion of bargaining starts from what I want; the religion of worship starts from who God is. At its close Paper 89 shows that when man comes to know God as one who can be trusted, the concepts of sacrifice and bargaining are transcended. Jesus taught that God is a Father who knows what we need before we ask. There is no reason to bargain with such a Father. We need only give thanks, love, and do his will. True worship is not a means of getting something; it is adoration that bursts forth when we recognize who God is and stand before his beauty. The Urantia Book says that worship is an activity that is its own end (see Paper 5).

This does not mean there are no promises in our relationship with God. The Urantia Book presents the covenant Melchizedek gave to Abraham: God does everything, and man has only to believe (see Paper 93). This is not bargaining but a relationship of trust. Our devotion and service, too, become true worship when they are not payments in hope of reward but a joyful response to the love already received.

Today, honestly examine whether a bargaining spirit hides in your prayers and service to God. Then take even a short time in which you ask for nothing and offer only gratitude and love. That is the beginning of worship beyond bargaining. In that time we stand before the Father not as merchants striking a deal but as beloved children.
d173.pr: Today, spend five minutes in prayer asking for nothing and offering only thanks and praise.

msg: The last section of Paper 89 discusses how people today should deal with the consciousness of sin. Today's passage offers a strikingly new perspective. The possibility of the recognition of the sense of guilt is a badge of transcendent distinction for mankind. It does not mark man as mean but rather sets him apart as a creature of potential greatness and ever-ascending glory. When our view of the sense of sin changes like this, the whole atmosphere of our spiritual life changes.

In many religious traditions, guilt has been regarded as proof of human wretchedness and worthlessness. Because of guilt, people hated themselves, trembled before God, and strove to lighten the burden through austerities and sacrifices. As the whole of Paper 89 shows, humanity has endured even bloody sacrifices and self-inflicted bodily harm to appease its sense of sin. But The Urantia Book sees guilt with entirely different eyes. Animals do not feel guilt. Only a being with a moral nature, one who recognizes something higher, can grieve at having fallen short of it.

Guilt, then, is evidence that we are beings called to something higher. The pain of knowing I have done wrong means that a sense of what is right is alive within me, and that sense is not unrelated to the Thought Adjuster who indwells us. The passage says that such a sense of unworthiness is the initial stimulus that should lead quickly and surely to those faith conquests which translate the mortal mind to the superb levels of moral nobility, cosmic insight, and spiritual living. The ache of conscience is not meant to put us down but is heaven's call to raise us up.

The key words here are quickly and surely. Guilt is not a place to stay but a door to pass through. It is not God's will that we linger in guilt condemning ourselves. Guilt fulfills its mission when it serves as a stimulus that turns us around and directs us toward God. In the very next paragraphs The Urantia Book says that divine forgiveness need not even be sought; one need only realize and accept that the relationship of loyalty has been restored (see Paper 89). The Father is always waiting for his children to return.

The passage ends thus: thus are all the meanings of human existence changed from the temporal to the eternal, and all values are elevated from the human to the divine. One who has turned to God through guilt is not the same person as before. Knowing his weakness, he is humble; knowing God's grace, he is grateful; and he is filled with longing for a higher life. The place where he fell becomes, instead, a new starting point. The experience of rising from failure later becomes the strength to understand and hold up a neighbor who has stumbled on the same road.

If some wrong weighs on your heart today, do not hide it or endlessly reproach yourself. Remember that this pain is a sign that you are called to a higher existence, and turn in faith to the Father. And if there is something you can set right, set it right today. The Father cares more about the road we will walk ahead than about our past.
d174.pr: Honestly confess to God one wrong that troubles you, and if it can be set right, act on it today.

msg: Paper 90 deals with the history of shamans, medicine men, and priests. At its opening, today's passage shows the whole course of religious evolution at a glance. Evolutionary religion is born of a simple and all-powerful fear, the fear which surges through the human mind when confronted with the unknown, the inexplicable, and the incomprehensible. But religion eventually achieves the profoundly simple realization of an all-powerful love. When the soul is awakened to the conception of the limitless affection of the Universal Father for the sons of the universe, that love sweeps irresistibly through the human soul.

From all-powerful fear to all-powerful love: this is the beginning and the end of religious evolution. The distance between these two points is vast indeed. Hundreds of thousands of years lie between the primitive man trembling before thunder and lightning and the believer who calls God a loving Father. Interestingly, the passage calls both emotions all-powerful. Fear can take complete hold of a person, and so can love. But fear makes people shrink, while love sets them free.

The passage says that in between the beginning and the consummation there intervene the long ages of the shamans, who presume to stand between man and God as intermediaries, interpreters, and intercessors. Because people thought they could not approach the gods directly, they relied on those said to have special powers. Shamans claimed to convey the will of the spirits; they performed rituals, healed the sick, and foretold the future. On the one hand this institution served to organize and preserve religion, but on the other it blocked people from approaching God for themselves. Dependence on intermediaries finally made religion the privilege of a few and kept ordinary people perpetual children.

One of the central truths of the gospel The Urantia Book proclaims is that no one now needs such an intermediary. The Universal Father directly indwells each person's mind through the Thought Adjuster. The Spirit of Truth has been poured out upon all people. Jesus taught that we may come directly to God, calling him Father. Anyone who opens his heart and seeks sincerely can meet God. Religious leaders and teachers remain precious, but they are not gatekeepers standing between God and us; they are only guides who walk the road with us.

Where along this journey does our faith stand today? If we still fear God and regard him as far away, we remain at an early stage of evolution. If we think we must go through someone else to approach God, the age of the shamans still lingers in our hearts. But when we realize that God is a Father who loves us infinitely, that love sweeps irresistibly through our souls and drives out all fear.

Today, speak directly to the Universal Father without any intermediary. No grand words are needed. Open your heart and talk to him as a beloved child talks to a father. Feel his limitless affection enfolding you now. In that moment we stand at the destination toward which the long journey of evolution was always heading: the religion of love.
d175.pr: In a quiet moment today, call the Universal Father your Father and pour out what is on your heart directly to him.

d176.t: Scaffolding That Has Served Its Purpose
msg: Paper 90 shows step by step how primitive people explained the causes of sickness and death. At first they attributed them to the influence of ghosts, then to violence or magic, then to punishment for breaking taboos, and at last they came to understand natural causes. Concluding this progression, today's passage offers a profound insight. Evolution unerringly achieves its end: it imbues man with that superstitious fear of the unknown and dread of the unseen which is the scaffolding for the God concept. In these words lies the comfort that even the dark periods of human history were not in vain.

Consider the metaphor of scaffolding. When workers construct a great building, they erect scaffolding around it. Without scaffolding they cannot lay bricks up high. But when the building is finished, the scaffolding is taken down. Left standing, it would hide the building's beauty and get in the way of those coming and going. So it was with the superstitious fear of primitive people. That fear made human beings conscious of the unseen world and led them to think about a being greater than themselves. It became the scaffolding for raising the edifice of the God concept.

The passage goes on to say that having witnessed the birth of an advanced comprehension of Deity, through the co-ordinate action of revelation, this same technique of evolution then unerringly sets in motion those forces of thought which will inexorably obliterate the scaffolding, which has served its purpose. What matters here is that evolution and revelation work together. Evolution prepares the human mind, and revelation shines higher truth into that prepared mind. Then, once truth has taken hold, evolution again clears away old superstitions through the power of reason and science.

This principle also applies to our personal growth in faith. The ideas about God we held in childhood were simple and sometimes mixed with fear. We may have imagined God as one who watches us from above the sky and punishes us when we do wrong. Even such ideas once served as scaffolding that made us conscious of God. But as faith grows, we must take that scaffolding down. Only then is the true face of God as a loving Father revealed. Just as clothes that fit a child do not fit an adult, our concepts of faith must be renewed as we grow.

When the scaffolding comes down, some fear that the building itself will collapse. As science clears away superstition, they feel that faith itself is being shaken. But as the passage says, the scaffolding is removed because the building is complete. When science erases old fears, true faith in God appears all the more clearly and beautifully. True faith does not lean on superstition; it grows firmer in the light of truth.

Today, consider what old scaffolding in your faith now needs to be taken down. If there are habits kept out of fear or notions followed without understanding, hold them up to the light of truth. Where the scaffolding has gone, the God of love will be seen more brightly. The courage to lay down the old in following truth is the mark of a growing faith.
d176.pr: Recall one fearful image of God you have carried since childhood, and meditate on replacing it with the truth of a loving Father.

msg: Paper 91 shows how prayer has evolved. The first prayers were not addressed to the gods but were monologues wishing for good luck. Primitive man thought aloud, conversing with an alter ego in his mind, and over the generations that alter ego was imagined as ghosts, fetishes, and spirits, and at last as gods. At the end of this long evolution, today's passage reveals a wonderful truth. Enlightened prayer must recognize not only an external and personal God but also an internal and impersonal Divinity, the indwelling Adjuster.

The passage acknowledges that it is altogether fitting that man, when he prays, should strive to grasp the concept of the Universal Father on Paradise. We look up to and worship the infinite Father at the center of the universe. But for most practical purposes, it says, there is a more effective technique: to revert to the concept of a near-by alter ego, just as the primitive mind was wont to do, and then to recognize that the idea of this alter ego has evolved from a mere fiction to the truth of God's indwelling mortal man in the factual presence of the Adjuster. The two approaches do not exclude each other; together they enrich our prayer.

This is a truly beautiful reversal. The alter ego with whom primitive people conversed in their imagination proves, in the light of revelation, to be an actually existing divine presence. Of course, the primitive alter ego was mostly a projection of their own minds. Yet the longing that sought a partner in conversation deep within the mind was not in vain. Now we know that a fragment of the Universal Father actually indwells us (see Paper 107). Prayer is not only crying out toward a distant heaven; it is also intimate conversation with the God within me.

The final sentence of the passage gives great comfort to our prayer life. Man can talk face to face, as it were, with a real and genuine and divine alter ego that indwells him and is the very presence and essence of the living God, the Universal Father. God is not so far away that our voices cannot reach him. He is nearer than our breath and deeper than our thoughts. The moment we quietly gather our hearts, we are already standing before him.

Such prayer is not bound by forms. Set words, places, or times are not required. Walking along the road, at work, or before going to bed, we can converse with the alter ego within. We can pour out our worries, express our thanks, ask for wisdom, and sometimes simply abide together without words. This daily habit of communion with the Adjuster is the path by which our thoughts and the Adjuster's thoughts gradually become one, and that is the path of the soul's growth. The Adjuster is our closest companion, who listens even to our smallest concerns.

Today, when you pray, do not look only to the far heavens; turn toward the depths of your own heart. Speak to the Father's spirit there as you would to your closest friend. Then be silent for a while and listen for his response. In that stillness we will realize that we are never alone.
d177.pr: Today, quietly close your eyes and tell the Adjuster within about your day, as you would your closest friend.

msg: After examining the many effects of prayer on the individual and on society, Paper 91 in today's passage tells us the most remarkable quality of prayer. The efficacy of prayer in the personal spiritual experience of the one who prays is in no way dependent on such a worshiper's intellectual understanding, philosophic acumen, social level, cultural status, or other mortal acquirements. The psychic and spiritual concomitants of the prayer of faith are immediate, personal, and experiential. This sentence declares that the door of prayer stands equally open to all.

These words are the exact opposite of the world's standards. In the world, the learned get more opportunities, those of high status wield greater influence, and the cultivated receive more respect. Even within religion it is easy to assume that those who know much theology or have long experience are closer to God. But The Urantia Book says such distinctions mean nothing in the realm of prayer. The earnest prayer of an unlettered grandmother and the prayer of a great scholar are equally precious before God.

The passage goes on to say that there is no other technique whereby every man, regardless of all other mortal accomplishments, can so effectively and immediately approach the threshold of that realm wherein he can communicate with his Maker. There the creature contacts with the reality of the Creator, with the indwelling Thought Adjuster. Prayer is a door open to everyone. Even without money, with little schooling, or without recognition in society, we can knock at that door at any time. That door is never locked.

This reveals God's fairness and love. The Universal Father has sent a Thought Adjuster equally to all his children. The same divine fragment indwells the mind of the king and the mind of the slave. Jesus, too, taught that God is no respecter of persons and that those with the heart of a little child enter the kingdom of God. What is needed to come to God is not knowledge or status but a sincere heart and a living faith. Heaven's door does not open by the world's standards; it opens to a sincere heart.

This does not mean that intelligence and learning are useless. Elsewhere The Urantia Book says that the content and level of prayer grow along with a person's understanding. But the efficacy of prayer, the experience of actual contact with God, does not depend on such things. So those who feel inadequate need not lose heart, and those who think they know much have no reason for pride. Before prayer we are all simply children of the Father alike. Indeed, the more one knows, the more one should strive to keep a heart as simple as a child's, so that knowledge does not become a stumbling block to meeting God.

Today, if you have felt unworthy to pray, lay that thought down. Come to God just as you are now. And remembering that God also hears with care the prayers of those you have ignored or looked down on, look upon your neighbors with a humble heart. Before the door of prayer we are all equal brothers and sisters.
d178.pr: Today, offer a short, unadorned prayer, and pray as well for a neighbor you have looked down on.

msg: Paper 92 shows how religion has developed along the two paths of evolution and revelation. Today's passage states an important principle about the nature of revelation. Revelation is evolutionary but always progressive. Down through the ages of a world's history, the revelations of religion are ever-expanding and successively more enlightening. And it is the mission of revelation to sort and censor the successive religions of evolution.

But the passage immediately makes clear the limits of revelation. If revelation is to exalt and upstep the religions of evolution, then must such divine visitations portray teachings which are not too far removed from the thought and reactions of the age in which they are presented. Thus must and does revelation always keep in touch with evolution, and always must the religion of revelation be limited by man's capacity of receptivity. The light of heaven is infinite, but the human vessel that receives it differs in size from age to age. Just as too bright a light blinds the eyes, truth that cannot be borne only confuses.

This principle is clearly seen in the five epochal revelations given to Urantia. The teachings of Dalamatia, the teachings of Eden, Melchizedek of Salem, Jesus of Nazareth, and the Urantia Papers were given in succession (see Paper 92). Each revelation contained as much truth as the people of its age could receive. Melchizedek taught salvation through faith and the one God, yet people found even that hard to bear. Jesus, too, told his disciples that he had many things to say to them, but they could not bear them now.

This truth gives us two lessons. First, we must not absolutize the revelation we have received. The truth we hold today was also given in accordance with the receptive capacity of this age, and greater light will come. The Urantia Book itself acknowledges that it contains the science of its time and will one day need revision. Second, we must be generous in understanding the faith of others. Each person's vessel for receiving truth is a different size. To respect their pace and wait for them is heaven's way. The more truth we have, the more patient we must be with those who cannot yet receive it.

This principle also applies to our personal spiritual growth. The Thought Adjuster and the Spirit of Truth illuminate truth for us as much as we can bear. When words we did not understand yesterday suddenly become clear today, it is because our vessel has grown a little in the meantime. So if we want to receive more truth, we must enlarge our vessel. Learning humbly, living out the truth we have received, and widening our hearts are the very preparation for greater revelation. The Spirit of Truth never hurries, and with every step we take he lights the next.

Today, consider which truths you have already received but have not yet lived out. When we walk by the light we have, greater light is given. And rather than judging those whose understanding differs from yours, keep a generous heart that respects the pace at which heaven is leading them. Heaven leads each of us as much as we can bear.
d179.pr: Choose one truth you already know but have not yet practiced, and live it out today.

msg: The last section of Paper 92 deals with how we should regard the world's many religions. Today's passage says that the many religions of Urantia are all good to the extent that they bring man to God and bring the realization of the Father to man. And it points out that it is a fallacy for any group of religionists to conceive of their creed as The Truth; such attitudes bespeak more of theological arrogance than of certainty of faith.

These words resonate deeply in a world where conflict between religions never ceases. Throughout history countless wars and persecutions have been waged in the name of religion. People believed that only their own faith was right and all others false, and they hated one another. But The Urantia Book plainly sets out the standard by which the worth of a religion is to be judged: does it lead people to God and bring them to realize his fatherhood? By this standard we can see that many religions, with differing names and forms, each play a good part.

The passage goes on to say that there is not a Urantia religion that could not profitably study and assimilate the best of the truths contained in every other faith, for all contain truth. As Papers 94 and 95 show, the teachings of Melchizedek spread to India and China, Egypt and Persia, leaving their traces in many religions. In the humility of Lao-tse, the morality of Confucius, the compassion of Buddha, and the righteousness of Ikhnaton, the light of truth from heaven is shining. When we have eyes to recognize that light, our own faith grows richer. Truth is not the possession of any one group; it is heaven's gift to all humanity.

The final sentence of the passage gives very practical guidance. Religionists would do better to borrow the best in their neighbors' living spiritual faith rather than to denounce the worst in their lingering superstitions and outworn rituals. When we look at other religions, we often fix our eyes on their weakest and strangest-looking parts. But that is not fair, for superstitions and outworn rituals linger in our own religion too. To see and learn from one another's best is the mark of a mature believer. To one who seeks humbly to learn, teachers appear everywhere.

This does not mean that all religions are the same or that there are no differences in truth. The Urantia Book says that the religion of Jesus, the gospel of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, is the highest truth given to humanity. But the more truth one holds, the more humble and generous one must be. Jesus said not to forbid one who does good even though he does not follow us. Certainty of truth should show itself not in condemning others but in loving them.

Today, think of a neighbor whose faith differs from yours, and find one beautiful thing in that faith worth learning. Then hold a grateful heart for it. In doing so we cross the walls of religion and live a little more deeply the truth that all people are children of the same Father. When we see one another as pilgrims walking toward the same Father, religion becomes not a cause of strife but a bridge of reconciliation.
d180.pr: Find and write down one thing worth emulating in the faith of someone whose beliefs differ from yours, and give thanks for it.

msg: Paper 93 tells the story of Machiventa Melchizedek, who appeared in the flesh on Urantia about two thousand years before Christ. He came as an emergency bestowal to guard the light of truth that was dying out after the default of Adam and Eve. Dwelling at Salem, he taught the one God and proclaimed the good news that salvation is obtained through faith. Today's passage sums up his mission in a word: Melchizedek prepared the way and set the monotheistic stage of world tendency for the bestowal of an actual Paradise Son of the one God.

Let us notice the phrase prepared the way. Melchizedek's mission was not complete in itself but was preparation for a greater work. He laid the groundwork in human minds so that when Michael, that is, Jesus, came, people would be able to understand him. Had Jesus come to a world with no concept of the one God, his teachings would hardly have been received. The seed Melchizedek sowed grew through Abraham, Moses, and the prophets, and at last prepared the stage for the coming of Jesus. His sojourn in the flesh lasted less than a hundred years, but the way he prepared endured for thousands.

The passage says that Melchizedek vividly portrayed this God as the Father of all, and represented him to Abraham as a God who would accept man on the simple terms of personal faith. In its day this was a revolutionary teaching. People believed that to win the gods' favor they had to offer gifts and sacrifices. But Melchizedek taught that God accepts people by faith alone. This simple gospel was so far ahead of its time that many could not understand it, yet the truth did not vanish but carried on. Because Abraham held fast to this truth, he is remembered by many today as the father of faith.

The passage's final sentence is moving. Michael, when he appeared on earth, confirmed all that Melchizedek had taught concerning the Paradise Father. Across a span of two thousand years the teachings of the two joined into one. Truth does not change with the passing of time. The God of love whom Melchizedek taught, the God who receives us by faith, was the same as the Father Jesus revealed. Though ages change and expressions differ, the heart of truth is always the same.

This story holds meaning for each of our lives as well. We too may be preparing the way for someone. Even if what I do today bears no great fruit right away, it may become the ground on which another receives truth later. The stories of God told to our children, the kindness shown to a friend, the service quietly rendered in our community accumulate unseen and will one day help someone's spiritual awakening. Even if we never see the fruit ourselves, sowing seed is never in vain. God's work is always like a relay race carried on across many generations.

Today, live with the awareness that your life is preparing the way for someone. Do not be disappointed even if there is no visible result. Just as the seed Melchizedek sowed blossomed two thousand years later, everything done in love and truth will surely bear fruit in God's time.
d181.pr: Today, sow a small seed of God's love in someone's life, and leave its fruit to God.

msg: At the heart of Paper 93 stands the covenant between Melchizedek and Abraham. Melchizedek told Abraham to count the stars of heaven and promised that his descendants would be as many; Abraham believed, and it was counted to him for righteousness. Today's passage reveals the meaning of this covenant. This covenant of Melchizedek with Abraham represents the great Urantian agreement between divinity and humanity whereby God agrees to do everything; man only agrees to believe God's promises and follow his instructions. Within this short covenant lies the whole secret of living by faith.

The structure of this covenant is truly astonishing. In an ordinary contract, both parties exchange things of equal value. But in this covenant God does everything, and man has only to believe and follow. It is a promise so favorable to man that it seems almost unfair. Yet that is exactly where the essence of God's love lies. God is not one who seeks to extract something from us but one who seeks to give us everything. Our part is only to trust and accept that love.

The passage says that heretofore it had been believed that salvation could be secured only by works, sacrifices and offerings. As we saw in Paper 89, humanity long bargained with the gods, trying to buy their favor with offerings. But Melchizedek again brought to Urantia the good news that salvation, favor with God, is to be had by faith. This is also the heart of the gospel Jesus later taught. The kingdom of God is not something bought by effort but a gift received by faith.

But the passage adds a sad fact as well. This gospel of simple faith in God was too advanced; the Semitic tribesmen subsequently preferred to go back to the older sacrifices and atonement for sin by the shedding of blood. Why did people abandon such good news? Perhaps because they felt secure only when they had offered something and made an effort. Paying the price themselves felt more certain than believing in a love freely given. This attitude lingers in us today too. Rather than receive grace, we want to feel that we have earned our worthiness.

A life of faith is not a life of doing nothing. In the covenant, man agrees to follow God's instructions. But that obedience is not a price paid to gain salvation; it is a response to love already received. A child who trusts the father finds joy in doing the father's will. Acts done grudgingly out of fear and acts done gladly out of love may look alike outwardly, but their roots are entirely different. That is why the life of faith is not a burden but freedom, not duty but joy.

Today, consider what you are striving to do in order to earn God's love. Then lay that burden down and believe that God has already promised to do everything. When we gladly follow his will on the foundation of that trust, we, like Abraham, enjoy the peace of being counted righteous by faith. Faith does not remove our share of effort, but it lifts fear and anxiety from that effort.
d182.pr: Set aside the striving to earn God's love, and gladly do one good deed in gratitude for the love already received.

msg: Paper 94 shows how the teachings of Melchizedek spread eastward and left their mark on the religious thought of India and China. In sixth-century B.C. China a great teacher named Lao-tse appeared. Building on the concepts of the Salem tradition, he taught that Tao was the One First Cause of all creation. Today's passage says that his understanding of the eternal purpose of God was clear, and it presents his teaching: The Absolute Deity does not strive but is always victorious; he does not coerce mankind but always stands ready to respond to their true desires.

The words does not strive but is always victorious beautifully express the way God rules. Worldly powers win by pushing with force and crushing their rivals. But God does not rule that way. He respects our free will and never drags us along against it. Just as water does not fight the rock but flows gently around it and in the end wears it away, God's will works quietly and patiently until it is at last fulfilled. The Urantia Book says that the will of God is eternal in patience and eternal in the inevitability of its expression.

The words that he does not coerce mankind but always stands ready to respond to their true desires are also a deep comfort. God waits for us to open our hearts. When we truly seek him and long for the good, he always responds. The Thought Adjuster, too, never oppresses us from within but gently leads us to choose the higher thing for ourselves. Because coerced love is not love, God waits for our free response. The patience of the God who waits shows the depth of his love.

The passage then gives Lao-tse's teaching about the true religionist. Expressing the truth that it is more blessed to give than to receive, he said that the good man seeks not to retain truth for himself but rather attempts to bestow these riches upon his fellows, for that is the realization of truth. Truth is not a treasure to hoard but a spring to let flow. When we share the truth we have received, it does not diminish; rather, it grows deeper within us. Jesus too taught: freely you have received, freely give.

Finally the passage says that the will of the Absolute God always benefits, never destroys; the purpose of the true believer is always to act but never to coerce. This shows how believers should live in the world. We must be active in doing good, but we must never force our convictions on others. The many historical tragedies in which people were oppressed and coerced in the name of religion were the result of forgetting this teaching. Just as God does not coerce us, we must not coerce our neighbors.

Today, look for the places where you are trying to gain something by striving and pushing. In your family, at work, or in your faith community, rather than forcing your will through, try doing good gently and patiently, as God does. And share without reserve the truth and love you have received. Love that does not strive wins in the end, in the deepest place.
d183.pr: Today, when you want to insist on your own way, step back and do good gently and patiently instead.

msg: After surveying in turn the development of Brahmanism and Hinduism in India, Taoism and Confucianism in China, and Buddhism, Paper 94 closes with today's passage. All Urantia is waiting for the proclamation of the ennobling message of Michael, unencumbered by the accumulated doctrines and dogmas of nineteen centuries of contact with the religions of evolutionary origin. And it declares that the hour is striking for presenting to Buddhism, to Christianity, to Hinduism, even to the peoples of all faiths, not the gospel about Jesus, but the living, spiritual reality of the gospel of Jesus.

The distinction between the gospel about Jesus and the gospel of Jesus is an important theme running through the whole of The Urantia Book. The gospel of Jesus is what Jesus himself taught: the good news that God is the Father of all people and that all people are brothers to one another. It is the simple yet profound truth that by faith we become sons and daughters of God. The gospel about Jesus, on the other hand, is the teaching people developed after his departure concerning his person, his death, and his resurrection. Paper 196 distinguishes between the religion of Jesus and the religion about Jesus, saying that people became so absorbed in worshiping Jesus that they lost the religion Jesus himself had (see Paper 196). The gospel of Jesus is the faith Jesus lived by; the gospel about Jesus is what people came to believe about him. Both are precious, but without the former, the latter loses its life.

The passage says that Michael's message has been encumbered by doctrines and dogmas accumulated over nineteen centuries. Upon Jesus' simple teachings were overlaid countless theological disputes, church institutions, and rituals borrowed from pagan religions. As a result, many people today encounter Christianity without ever meeting the living gospel of Jesus. Especially for those of other religious traditions, the doctrinal system of Western Christianity feels foreign and hard to accept.

But the gospel of Jesus itself is foreign to no people or culture. That God is a loving Father, that all people are brothers and sisters, that by faith we can enter into a living relationship with God: these are truths that can touch the hearts of Buddhists, Hindus, and Muslims alike. As we have seen, the seeds of truth Melchizedek sowed are already growing within their traditions. The gospel of Jesus can become the light that brings those seeds to completion.

These words give us a mission. To proclaim the gospel of Jesus is not to tear down another's religion and pull them into my denomination. It is to show the life Jesus lived, a life of trusting God and loving one's neighbor. It means practicing love rather than arguing doctrine, sharing living faith rather than imposing forms. Then the gospel of Jesus can cross the walls of religion and reach every human heart.

Today, consider whether your faith rests in doctrines about Jesus or whether you are living out the religion Jesus lived. And strive to make this a day when your life, more than your words, proclaims the gospel of Jesus. The starting point is to make the faith with which Jesus trusted God your own faith.
d184.pr: Today, rather than speaking of doctrine, do one loving act Jesus would have done for a neighbor of another faith.

msg: Paper 95 shows how the teachings of Melchizedek spread through the Levant, that is, Mesopotamia and Egypt, Persia and Arabia. In the section on Egypt, today's passage states an important principle. Moral evolution is not wholly dependent on revelation. High moral concepts can be derived from man's own experience, and man can even evolve spiritual values and derive cosmic insight from his personal experiential living. The reason, it says, is that a divine spirit indwells him.

These words show a deep trust in human beings. Even among those who have received no revelation and have never read a scripture, morality and spirituality can grow. Thousands of years before the Salem gospel arrived, Egypt had already developed ideals of justice, fairness, and truth. This was not because they had received special revelation but because they learned through the experience of life what is right and what is wrong. And beneath that learning lay the guidance of the divine spirit indwelling them.

Here we are led to reconsider the universal ministry of the Thought Adjuster. The Adjuster does not come only to those who believe in a particular religion. He indwells the mind of every normal human being capable of moral choice. That is why, in every people and every culture, there arise those who seek to live good lives by following the voice of conscience. Even without knowing God's name exactly, they love justice, mercy, and truth, and live close to the will of God. God was at work in human hearts even before revelation. To honor the small voice of conscience is to honor the spirit of God within me.

This does not mean that revelation is unnecessary. The passage adds that such natural evolutions of conscience and character were also augmented by the periodic arrival of teachers of truth, in ancient times from the second Eden, later on from Melchizedek's headquarters at Salem. Morality that grows from experience is lifted higher when it meets revelation. It is like a tree growing on its own that bears richer fruit once it receives the gardener's care. Evolution and revelation do not compete; they cooperate in leading humanity to God.

This truth has practical meaning for our daily lives. Each of our ordinary experiences can become material for spiritual growth. Through failures and wounds, joys and encounters, work and relationships, we learn what is truly valuable. Through those experiences the Adjuster gives us cosmic insight. So no moment of life is spiritually meaningless. Not only in the temple but in the kitchen, the workplace, and the street, our souls are growing. Two people may go through the same event; the one who reflects on it gains wisdom, while the one who lets it slip by gains nothing. The habit of reflecting on experience is the secret of spiritual growth.

Today, recall one past experience that taught you an important moral lesson. Meditate on how the divine spirit within you taught you through that experience. And keep a wide heart that recognizes the same spirit at work in the good conscience of neighbors whose faith differs from yours or who have no faith at all.
d185.pr: Write down a moral lesson you learned from something you recently went through, and thank the indwelling spirit who gave you that insight.

msg: Paper 95 introduces Amenemope, a great teacher of Egypt. A wise man who embraced the teachings of Melchizedek, he preserved both the ethics of evolution and the morals of revelation and passed them on to later ages. Today's passage summarizes his central teachings. This wise man of the Nile taught that riches take themselves wings and fly away, that all things earthly are evanescent. His great prayer was to be saved from fear. He exhorted all to turn away from the words of men to the acts of God. In substance he taught: Man proposes but God disposes.

The words that riches take themselves wings and fly away are vivid even today. We spend much time and heart gathering and guarding our possessions. But one economic crisis, one accident, one illness can make all we have gathered vanish in an instant. Amenemope taught us to face this fact squarely. This does not mean despising wealth. In the paragraph just before, he taught that riches and fortune are gifts of God (see Paper 95). He simply urged us not to bind our hearts to them but to hold fast to eternal values.

It is significant that his great prayer was to be saved from fear. The religion of the ancients was mostly gripped by fear. Fear of ghosts, fear of bad luck, fear of the wrath of the gods weighed heavily on life. Amenemope believed that by trusting God one could be freed from that fear. This flows in the same stream as the fear-destroying gospel Melchizedek proclaimed. One who knows that earthly things are fleeting and who trusts God has no reason to fear losing them.

His exhortation to turn away from the words of men to the acts of God is also precious. We care too much about how others judge us and what the world calls success. The words of men change from moment to moment and toss us this way and that. But the acts of God, his faithfulness revealed in creation and providence, do not change. When we look to them, we gain a center that does not waver. The saying that man proposes but God disposes humbles our plans and releases us from clinging to outcomes. The faith that planning is our part while the outcome is in God's hands keeps us from collapsing even in the face of failure.

The passage says that Amenemope's teachings, translated into Hebrew, determined the philosophy of the Old Testament Book of Proverbs, and translated into Greek, they gave color to all subsequent Hellenic religious philosophy. The wisdom of one man flowed across many peoples and ages. Truth knows no borders, and God has taught humanity through teachers of many peoples. That the voice of an Egyptian sage is contained in the wisdom of the Proverbs we read reminds us once again that God's truth is not the exclusive property of any one people.

Today, consider what earthly things you are holding too tightly. Then entrust to God the fear of losing them. Plan and work with all your might, but enjoy the peace of trusting God to dispose of the outcome. That trust is the deliverance from fear that Amenemope sought.
d186.pr: Today, write down one worry, and pray over it by separating the part where you will do your best from the part you will entrust to God.

msg: Paper 96 tells how the Hebrews came to understand their God, Yahweh. At first Yahweh was a rough nature god associated with the volcano of Mount Sinai. Moses labored heroically to lift this tribal deity toward the Most High God whom Melchizedek had taught. Today’s passage points to the most unique and amazing feature of Hebrew religious history: the continuous evolution of the concept of Deity from the primitive god of Mount Horeb, up through the teachings of their successive spiritual leaders, to the Deity doctrines of the Isaiahs, who proclaimed that magnificent concept of the loving and merciful Creator Father.

These words teach us far more than a fact of religious history; they reveal something about the very nature of faith. God himself does not change. But man’s understanding of God grows. The Yahweh the Hebrews first knew was a jealous and wrathful god of war who struck down his enemies. Yet through Samuel and Elijah, Amos and Hosea, Micah and Jeremiah, and finally the Isaiahs, that understanding widened and deepened into a God of justice, a God of love, the Father who is Creator of the whole universe (see Paper 97).

This evolution was possible because every age had its courageous spiritual leaders. They were not content with the common understanding of their day; they laid hold of a higher truth. At times they met the opposition of priests and kings and were ignored by the people. After Moses died, the lofty concept he had taught quickly declined, and the people went back to the golden calf. But the spark of truth never went out. When one man fell, another rose up and carried the flame forward. Truth reaches beyond any single lifetime, passing from generation to generation and growing a little brighter each time.

The Urantia Book teaches that we should read the Hebrew scriptures with this evolutionary perspective in mind. The portraits of God in the Bible are not all on the same level. Some passages show a primitive tribal deity; others come close to the loving Father whom Jesus revealed. If we fail to see this and accept every verse as equally true, we fall into confusion. But once we understand the flow of this evolution, we can see in the scriptures a majestic journey in which the understanding of God grows ever brighter.

The same principle applies to our personal faith. Each of us must grow in our understanding of God. If we are still holding on to the picture of God we had as children, our faith has stalled. As we pray, worship, study truth, and experience God in daily life, our concept of God grows broader and deeper. We walk within our own lifetime the road the Hebrew people traveled over many centuries. At the end of that road stands the loving Father whom Jesus showed us. Living faith refuses to stay with yesterday’s understanding and moves on today toward a greater light.

Today, quietly write down what kind of God you understand God to be right now. Then hold that understanding up against the Father whom Jesus revealed, and see how close it comes. If fear and severity still linger there, take time to picture him anew as the Father of love and mercy.
d187.pr: Write down three words that describe God as you see him, and compare them with the Father whom Jesus revealed.

d188.t: The Psalms: A Record of the God Concept
msg: The last section of Paper 96 deals with two books of Hebrew scripture, the Psalms and Job. Of the Psalms today’s passage says that no collection of religious writings gives expression to such a wealth of devotion and inspirational ideas of God as the Book of Psalms. It adds that it would be very helpful if, in reading this wonderful collection of worshipful literature, consideration could be given to the source and chronology of each separate hymn of praise and adoration, since no other single collection covers such a great range of time.

The passage tells us that the Book of Psalms is the record of the varying concepts of God entertained by the believers of the Salem religion throughout the Levant, and that it embraces the entire period from Amenemope to Isaiah. We often think of the Psalms as the work of one man, David, but in fact they are a collection of praises and prayers left by countless believers from many eras and many lands. Some came from the wisdom of Egypt, some from the Salem missionaries of Mesopotamia, and some were written by the prophets of the exile. The Psalms are not the song of a single voice but a chorus sung together by many generations.

And so in the Psalms God is depicted in all phases of conception, from the crude idea of a tribal deity to the vastly expanded ideal of the later Hebrews. Some psalms cry out for enemies to be destroyed and vengeance to be taken. Some portray God as jealous and wrathful. But others sing of God as shepherd and refuge, as a loving ruler and merciful Father. In those lofty psalms where Yahweh is pictured as a loving ruler and merciful Father, we catch an early glimpse of the God whom Jesus would reveal. The very fact that such varied pictures of God stand side by side in one book is evidence that the concept of God has grown.

This perspective gives us great freedom as we read the Psalms. We need not receive every line of every psalm with equal authority. When we read a psalm that curses enemies, we can understand it as the honest cry of an ancient believer in anguish, without taking it as the will of God. On the other hand, a psalm such as the confession “⟦Q 131:2.7⟧The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want⟦/Q⟧” can carry our own hearts to God just as it is. Read with discernment, the Psalms become an even more living book of prayer.

The Psalms also show us the many paths of worship. There are songs of joyful praise, deep laments, and prayers that pour out doubt and anger without disguise. The psalmists did not dress up their feelings; they brought them to God just as they were. This is permission for us, too, to be honest before God. God receives not only our joy but our sorrow and confusion as well. And in such honest prayer our concept of God steadily grows.

Today, choose one psalm and read it slowly. Notice what kind of God it portrays, and find within it a line that sings of the Father of love and mercy, and make that line your prayer for today. When the songs of ancient believers become our songs, we are joined to a worshiping community thousands of years old.
d188.pr: Choose a psalm today, find a line that sings of the God of love and mercy, and pray with it.

msg: Paper 97 tells how the concept of God evolved through the Hebrew prophets. Samuel proclaimed the unchanging God, Elijah the oneness of Yahweh, Amos the God of justice, and Hosea the God of love. Today’s passage shows the heart of the message Micah delivered in that unfolding story. He asks, “⟦Q 97:5.6⟧Shall I come before God with burnt offerings? Will the Lord be pleased with a thousand rams or with ten thousand rivers of oil?⟦/Q⟧” And he answers that what the Lord requires of man is “⟦Q 97:5.6⟧to do justly and to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God.⟦/Q⟧”

This question and answer overturn in a single stroke a history of sacrifice thousands of years long. As we saw in Paper 89, mankind long offered sacrifices to win the favor of the gods, even sacrificing their own children. Micah’s question includes the words “⟦Q 97:5.6⟧Shall I give my first-born for my transgression?⟦/Q⟧” because such a custom actually existed. But Micah declares that what God desires is not the blood of beasts, nor costly oil, nor the lives of children. What God desires is a changed life.

To do justly is to deal fairly with one’s neighbor: not to exploit the weak, to defend the rights of the poor, to trade without deceit. Micah sternly rebuked rulers who judged for bribes and priests who taught for hire (see Paper 97). To love mercy is to show kindness to others not as a duty but as a joy. If justice is fairness, mercy is love that goes beyond fairness. And to walk humbly with God is a life of daily companionship with him, seeking his will. These three become a mirror in which we can measure the genuineness of our own faith today.

These three are not separate from one another. The one who walks humbly with God naturally comes to do justly and love mercy. On the other hand, to demand justice without a relationship with God easily slides into self-righteousness, and to stress mercy alone easily drifts into sentimentality. The three that Micah set forth are the balanced shape of true religion. When Jesus later taught us to love God and to love our neighbor as ourselves, he carried forward this same spirit.

The passage says that it was a great age, that these were indeed stirring times when mortal man heard, and some even believed, such emancipating messages more than two and a half millenniums ago. Yet it laments that but for the stubborn resistance of the priests, these teachers would have overthrown the whole bloody ceremonial of Hebrew worship. Institutions and vested interests always stand in the way of the advance of truth. Even today, form and ritual sometimes try to take the place of a changed heart. We easily assume we have fulfilled our religious duty by attending worship and giving an offering. But Micah’s question is still being put to us.

Today, hold Micah’s three requirements up to your own life. Ask yourself whether you treated someone fairly today, whether you showed kindness gladly, and whether you walked humbly, seeking God’s will. Then pick one area where you fell short and resolve to do a little better tomorrow. What pleases God is not a grand offering but small, sincere changes like these in the way we live.
d189.pr: Choose one of justice, mercy, or a humble walk with God today, and decide on one concrete act that puts it into practice.

msg: The summit of Paper 97 is the teaching of the second Isaiah, who appeared during the Babylonian captivity. The Urantia Book says that from Machiventa to the time of Jesus no prophet or religious teacher reached the height of the concept of God that the second Isaiah attained (see Paper 97). Today’s passage tells us that this preacher of a supernal God never ceased to proclaim the God of love, and it shares his words of comfort: “⟦Q 97:7.12⟧I dwell in the high and holy place, also with him who is of a contrite and humble spirit.⟦/Q⟧”

These words hold God’s transcendence and his immanence in a single sentence. God dwells in the high and holy place. He is Creator of the entire universe, the infinite One at the eternal center of Paradise. Yet at the same time he dwells within the heart of the contrite and humble. The Highest is found in the lowliest place. The Urantia Book makes this truth even clearer through the indwelling of the Thought Adjuster: the infinite Father has sent a fragment of himself into the mind of each of us.

Notice here the condition: a contrite and humble spirit. A proud heart has no room for God to dwell. Those who think themselves sufficient feel no need of God. But those who know their own lack and have humbled their hearts have room to receive him. The Jews carried into captivity, having lost everything, were in just such a place. They had lost their temple and their nation, but in that lowly place they learned that God was not confined to the temple but dwelt in the humble heart. Humility is not belittling oneself; it is honestly acknowledging what we truly are before God.

The passage goes on to give further words of comfort: “⟦Q 97:7.12⟧And the Lord will guide you continually and satisfy your soul. You shall be like a watered garden and like a spring whose waters fail not.⟦/Q⟧” And it promises that if the enemy shall come in like a flood, the spirit of the Lord will lift up a defense against him. These words were a great hope to captives sunk in despair, and they have comforted countless people ever since. The soul that walks with God becomes not a parched land but a watered garden. Guidance, satisfaction, and protection: these three promises hold just as true for us today.

The last sentence of the passage sums it all up: once again the fear-destroying gospel of Melchizedek and the trust-breeding religion of Salem shone forth for the blessing of mankind. The gospel of faith that Melchizedek gave to Abraham, a light that had grown dim over long ages, shone out brightly again in the darkness of the exile. Truth never vanishes entirely. Even in the darkest times God raises up someone to rekindle it. And at last that truth was fully revealed in Jesus.

If today you feel, amid the hardships of life, as though you have lost everything, remember that this very lowly place is where you meet God. Humble your heart and come to him. He who dwells in the high and holy place dwells with you in your heart right now, and he will water your soul like a spring whose waters fail not.
d190.pr: Humble your heart today, confess your shortcomings to God, and then rest for a moment in the peace of the One who dwells within you.

msg: Paper 98 recounts the long journey of the Melchizedek teachings as they flowed into the Western world, passing through Greek philosophy, the Roman state religion, and the various mystery cults, until at last they reached Christianity. Along the way the Greeks sought security of mind through rigorous thinking, but the philosophers made light of worship, and the masses flocked to mystery cults that stirred the emotions. Today’s passage looks back on this history and draws out a principle: religions have long endured without philosophical support, but few philosophies, as such, have long persisted without some identification with religion.

This is not a disparagement of philosophy. The passage compares the relation of philosophy to religion with that of conception to action. Conception explains action and gives it direction, but it is action that actually lives and moves. In the same way, religion is the living experience of knowing God, and philosophy is the work of thought that seeks to understand and order that experience. Philosophy without experience, however refined, cannot hold a human life together; in the end it scatters into barren speculation. This is why the brilliant philosophy of Greece failed to win the hearts of ordinary people (see Paper 98, section 2).

Nor does this mean that religion may remain thoughtless. The passage clearly portrays the ideal human estate: that in which philosophy, religion, and science are welded into a meaningful unity by the conjoined action of wisdom, faith, and experience. Science deals with facts, philosophy weaves meanings, and religion experiences values. When these three do not push one another away but live in harmony within one personality, a person becomes whole, with head and heart no longer divided. The integration of personality that Papers 103 and 112 repeatedly stress points in exactly this direction.

In daily life this teaching returns to us as very concrete questions. Am I using faith as an excuse to stop thinking? Or am I so busy piling up and weighing knowledge that I keep postponing my living communion with God? Faith without wisdom easily leans toward superstition and dogmatism; knowledge without faith easily falls into cynicism and emptiness. And without experience, both faith and knowledge become mere words.

This principle holds just as true today. The modern world has made astonishing scientific progress, yet in the midst of all that knowledge many people lose the meaning of life and wander. On the other side, some religious people treat science and philosophy as enemies and build walls against them, shutting their faith inside a narrow fence. The Urantia Book urges us to move beyond both of these paths. Only when the honesty of science that respects facts, the sincerity of philosophy that seeks meaning, and the vitality of religion that experiences God come together does a person begin to see the universe rightly. This unity is not won merely by reading many books; it comes little by little as wisdom, faith, and experience grow together day by day.

So today, let us practice examining honestly in thought what we believe, looking again at what we know in the light of faith, and carrying both into some small action. Living experience of God deepens our thinking, and deeper thinking in turn makes our experience clearer. The lesson the Western world learned with such difficulty over thousands of years we can learn anew each day in the small choices of a single day.
d191.pr: Think honestly today about one thing you believe, and carry that belief into one small action.

msg: The last section of Paper 98, in dealing with the origins of Christianity, first corrects a very important point. The Creator Son, Michael, came to Urantia in the likeness of mortal flesh not to reconcile an angry God. He came rather to win all mankind to the recognition of the Father’s love and to the realization of their sonship with God. This brief paragraph touches the very foundation of faith: what kind of God we know and live by.

Reading Paper 98 as a whole, we can see why this correction was needed. As the teachings of Jesus spread westward, they became mixed with the Mithraic cult, the various mysteries, and ideas of blood sacrifice and atonement. The mystery cults taught of gods who died and rose again, of purification by blood, and of rites to appease angry deities, and these ideas gradually overlaid the simple gospel of Jesus. As a result many came to misunderstand God as a judge to be feared, one who forgives only when the price of blood is paid.

Yet the passage says that even the great advocate of the atonement doctrine realized something of this truth, for he declared that “⟦Q 98:7.1⟧God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.⟦/Q⟧” It was not God who needed to be reconciled but the human heart that had wandered away from him. God was the loving Father from the very beginning, and the Son revealed that love in a life that people could see and touch. Paper 103 says plainly that Jesus swept away all the rituals of sacrifice and atonement (see Paper 103, section 4).

This teaching gives great freedom to our life of faith. We do not pray and worship to soothe the temper of an angry God. We do so to respond with gratitude and trust to the Father who already loves us as his children. Even when we have done wrong, we need not hide to escape punishment. We need only return honestly, as a child returns to his father. Religion born of fear makes people shrink, but religion that has discovered love lifts them up.

We can learn one more thing from this history: as truth is passed along, it is hard to avoid having the ideas of the age attached to it. Paper 98 says that as the original teachings of Jesus entered the West they were Occidentalized, and in the process much was lost. That does not mean Christianity is without value. The life and teachings of Jesus still live within it, and it has led countless people to God. But we must strip away the husks that have gathered and return to the Father whom Jesus himself showed us: the father who sees the prodigal son from afar and runs to embrace him.

Today, let us look at the picture of God we carry in our hearts. Do we still think of God as someone whose mood we must watch, who opens his heart only grudgingly when we offer him something? The Father whom Jesus revealed is the one who comes to us first, forgives first, and loves first. Those who have grasped that love naturally pass it on to others. This is how we fulfill in our own lives the true purpose for which the Creator Son came into this world.
d192.pr: Picture God not as a fearsome judge but as a loving Father, and offer three prayers of thanksgiving today.

d193.t: True Religion on an Ordinary Day
msg: Paper 99 considers the role religion must play amid rapid social change. When machine civilization and the spread of knowledge shake the world and old institutions totter, the paper teaches, religion should devote itself less to designing a new social order directly and more to stabilizing the individual soul and safeguarding ideals. Today’s passage defines, briefly and powerfully, what true religion is in such an age of upheaval: true religion is a meaningful way of living dynamically face to face with the commonplace realities of everyday life.

The phrase to notice in this definition is commonplace realities. Religion is not found only in special places or special moments. It must live and move in all the ordinary hours of life: getting up in the morning and going to work, cooking meals, caring for children, clashing with coworkers, and ending the day with a tired body. And that encounter must be dynamic. It means not fleeing reality or resigning ourselves to it, but walking right into the middle of it as people who know God.

The passage then names three dangers religion must avoid. If religion is to stimulate individual development of character and augment integration of personality, it must not be standardized. If it is to stimulate evaluation of experience and serve as a value-lure, it must not be stereotyped. If religion is to promote supreme loyalties, it must not be formalized. A religion in which everyone believes according to the same mold, which never changes a method once fixed, and which keeps only outward rituals cannot help people grow. This is why Paper 99 repeatedly points out the weaknesses of institutional religion (see Paper 99, sections 2 and 6).

This teaching invites each of us to look at our own habits of faith. If our prayers have become the repetition of the same words, if our worship is filled only with a sense of duty, if our faith has become a matter of doing what others do, then our religion has quietly become standardized, stereotyped, and formalized. Habits themselves are not bad. As Paper 100 says, good religious habits help spiritual growth. But living experience and fresh meaning must flow within those habits.

Paper 99 also explains why such religion is especially needed today. When society changes rapidly and economic insecurity and clashing ideologies shake people, what they need most is an unshakable inner center. Just after our passage the paper says that whatever upheavals may attend the social and economic growth of civilization, religion will survive if it is genuine and worthy. It adds that in the end conduct is determined not so much by what a person knows as by what he believes (see Paper 99, section 4). Only a living religion that faces the realities of everyday life can hold people steady in such times.

Let us not let today slip by as just another ordinary day, but live it as a day faced together with God. We can be grateful even while washing the dishes, keep a brotherly spirit even in a difficult conversation, and find the value of faithfulness even in tedious work. As ordinary moments are transformed in this way into the experience of knowing God, our religion will be an anchor that holds no matter how the world is shaken. The ordinary day is the most honest test of whether our religion is true, and at the same time the place where we can meet God most closely.
d193.pr: Choose the most ordinary and tedious task of your day, and do it with care, as something done together with God.

d194.t: Knowing the Father, Knowing the Brother
msg: The fifth section of Paper 99 deals with the social aspect of religion. The passage first makes clear that religion is exclusively a personal spiritual experience: knowing God as a Father. No one can do it for us, and no group can hand it down to us wholesale. Yet as the corollary of that very personal experience, we come to know others as brothers. If God is my Father, he is also the Father of the person beside me.

So religion begins within and flows outward. Religion is first an inner or personal adjustment, and then it becomes a matter of social service or group adjustment. Those who stand in right relationship with God naturally strive to live in harmony with others as well. Because human beings are gregarious, religious groups will inevitably come into existence, and what happens to them depends very much on intelligent leadership. And religion, the passage says, has always been a conservator of morals and a stabilizer of society.

The paragraph that follows leaves us a sentence to keep always in mind: “⟦Q 99:5.2⟧True religion is to know God as your Father and man as your brother.⟦/Q⟧” It adds that religion is not a slavish belief in threats of punishment or magical promises of future mystical rewards. A faith that clings to fear and reward makes people slaves, but a faith that knows the Father and the brother makes people sons and daughters, members of one family. This was the heart of the kingdom of God that Jesus taught.

This teaching becomes a simple and clear measure of the genuineness of our faith. If we say we love God yet look down on people, our faith is only half a faith. On the other hand, if we are zealous only in helping people and have no living relationship with God, that service will not last long; it easily wears out or dries up (see Paper 99, section 1). The experience of knowing the Father and the life of serving our brothers go together like the root and the fruit of one tree.

Here we can also reconsider the meaning of religious groups. Paper 99 says that the socialization of religion has a true purpose. A community that gathers to worship, encourages one another, and shares truth protects and nurtures the faith of each person. But it warns that as religion becomes institutionalized, its power for good is lessened while its possibilities for evil are increased (see Paper 99, section 6). If a community is to stay alive, there must always be at its center each person’s living experience of God, and that experience must overflow in love toward the brothers outside its walls. A fellowship of those who know the Father should be not a fence that shuts people in but a starting point for serving the world.

Today, let us practice seeing everyone we meet as children of the same Father. Family or coworker, stranger or someone who thinks differently from us, all of them are children whom the Universal Father loves. When we remember this, our tone of voice changes, our patience grows longer, and forgiveness comes more easily. Discovering our brothers day by day in this way is also the path to knowing the Father more deeply. May this simple truth, knowing God as Father and man as brother, become a light that renews every relationship in our lives.
d194.pr: Think of one person who makes you uneasy today, and pray for that person, remembering that he or she is a child of the same Father.

d195.t: The Root and Fruit of Spiritual Growth
msg: Paper 100 deals with how religious living grows. It warns that some people are too busy to grow and so are in grave danger of spiritual fixation (see Paper 100, section 1). Today’s passage sums up in two points what spiritual development depends on: first, the maintenance of a living spiritual connection with true spiritual forces, and second, the continuous bearing of spiritual fruit, yielding the ministry to one’s fellows of that which has been received from one’s spiritual benefactors.

These two are like breathing in and breathing out. If the connection with God is broken, there is nothing to share; if we only receive and never share, what we have received stagnates and spoils. The soul grows when we keep our hearts open to God through prayer and worship and at the same time let the love and truth we receive flow out to our neighbors. The passage also tells us what this growth is built upon: the intellectual recognition of spiritual poverty, the self-consciousness of perfection-hunger, the desire to know God and be like him, and the wholehearted purpose to do the will of the Father in heaven.

The next paragraph shows the order of spiritual growth. Spiritual growth is first an awakening to needs, next a discernment of meanings, and then a discovery of values. The moment we realize that something is lacking in us is the starting point of growth. Those who think themselves already sufficient do not grow. And the evidence of true spiritual development is seen in a life motivated by love, activated by unselfish ministry, and dominated by the wholehearted worship of the perfection ideals of divinity.

The passage says that this entire experience constitutes the reality of religion as contrasted with mere theological beliefs. Knowing a great deal of doctrine is not the same as having grown. Only when loving motives, serving hands, and a worshiping heart show themselves in our lives are we truly growing. Paper 100 teaches that we cannot directly cause growth, but we can supply favorable conditions for it (see Paper 100, section 3). Connection and sharing are exactly those conditions.

It is worth reflecting one by one on the four foundations in the passage. To recognize our spiritual poverty is to leave self-righteousness behind and become humble. To hunger for perfection is to refuse to settle for who we are now and to press on toward a better self. The desire to know God and be like him gives growth its direction, and the wholehearted purpose to do the Father’s will binds all of these together. These four are also the very things the Thought Adjuster ceaselessly awakens within us. Our part is not to ignore that inner call but to answer it in the choices of each day.

Today, let us check two things. Did I set aside quiet time today for a living connection with God? And did I share with someone the grace I received today? If we do not put these two off with the excuse of busyness, we will grow, unseen but surely. Spiritual growth does not happen overnight, but it quietly builds up through the connecting and sharing of each day. Today’s small connections and small acts of sharing will one day ripen into the fruit of a mature personality shining with love, service, and worship.
d195.pr: Spend ten minutes in quiet communion with God today, then share with one person the comfort or insight you received.

msg: The last section of Paper 100 finds the summit of religious living in Jesus. It portrays his traits one after another. He was unfailingly kind, yet strong; easy to approach, yet unshaken in principle; always a well-balanced personality. His courage was paired with patience, his cheerfulness with the strength to bear deep sorrow, and his reverence with an easy simplicity that delighted in little children. Today’s passage gathers all of this into one sentence: Jesus was the perfectly unified human personality.

A unified personality is one whose inner and outer life are one, whose words and life are one, and whose many abilities and feelings are harmonized under a single purpose. We are often pulled in different directions. What we want and what we ought to do differ; what we believe and what we do are at odds; the face we show to others differs from the face we wear when alone. Jesus was not like that. Everything about him was gathered around one center: doing the Father’s will.

The passage says that today, as in Galilee, he continues to unify mortal experience and to co-ordinate human endeavors. He unifies life, ennobles character, and simplifies experience. A tangled and complicated life becomes simple when it places him at its center. He enters the human mind to elevate, transform, and transfigure it. And so the passage testifies that it is literally true: “⟦Q 100:7.18⟧If any man has Christ Jesus within him, he is a new creature; old things are passing away; behold, all things are becoming new.⟦/Q⟧”

Notice here the language of process: old things are passing away, and all things are becoming new. Transformation is not an event completed in a moment but a process that continues day by day. Even though we have not reached perfect unification as Jesus did, we can become a little more whole as we look to him. As Paper 100 says, the average mortal cannot hope to attain the perfection of Jesus, yet by following his life we can grow to resemble his character (see Paper 100, section 7).

The unified personality of Jesus was not given to us merely to be admired from a distance. The passage says that he still enters the human mind today. His spirit, the Spirit of Truth, has been poured out upon all people, and within us dwells the Thought Adjuster, the spirit of the Father. When we meditate on his life and try to live in his way, these spiritual helps gather our scattered thoughts and feelings into one. Unification is not something we force by willpower alone; it is something he works out within us when we open our hearts.

Today, let us look for one divided part of ourselves. There may be a place where we speak of love yet act coldly, or where we say we trust yet are gripped by worry. Invite Jesus into that place, and quietly ask what he would have done. As we gather our lives, one part at a time, under his center, life becomes simpler, our hearts grow peaceful, and we too grow as creatures who are being made new. The way of becoming like him is not a heavy burden but a path of becoming a little freer and more joyful each day.
d196.pr: Find one area of your life where your words and actions do not match, ask what Jesus would have done, and put it into practice.

d197.t: The Spirit Meets Us in Thought
msg: Paper 101 deals with the real nature of religion. It says that true religion is not a philosophical system of belief that can be reasoned out or replaced by something else, but a living experience produced as the Thought Adjuster, the spirit of the Universal Father, works within the human mind. Today’s passage tells us where in us that experience takes place: the divine spirit makes contact with mortal man, not by feelings or emotions, but in the realm of the highest and most spiritualized thinking.

This overturns the common religious assumptions of many people. We often think we have met God only when there are fervent emotions, tears, and overwhelming feelings. But the passage says clearly: “⟦Q 101:1.3⟧It is your thoughts, not your feelings, that lead you Godward.⟦/Q⟧” Emotions rise and fall like the weather. On days when we feel good God seems near, and on gloomy days he seems far away. But the spirit of God does not come and go with our moods.

Yet this thinking does not mean cold calculation or the piling up of knowledge. The passage says that the divine nature may be perceived only with the eyes of the mind, and adds that the mind that really discerns God, that hears the indwelling Adjuster, is the pure mind. It also quotes the words “⟦Q 101:1.3⟧Without holiness no man may see the Lord.⟦/Q⟧” The thinking that reaches God is honest, clean, and directed toward what is high. The passage calls all such inner and spiritual communion spiritual insight.

The last sentence of the passage explains how religious experience arises. Such religious experiences result from the impress made upon the mind of man by the combined operations of the Adjuster and the Spirit of Truth as they function amid and upon the ideas, ideals, insights, and spirit strivings of the evolving sons of God. The paragraph just before says that the Adjuster has no special mechanism through which to gain self-expression (see Paper 101, section 1). The Adjuster works through our ordinary thoughts and ideals. So the quality of the thoughts we entertain becomes the quality of the channel through which God can work within us.

This teaching reminds us how important it is to cultivate our thinking. If we fill our minds all day with resentment, worry, and thoughts that belittle others, the room in which the Adjuster can work grows narrow. But when we think on truth, beauty, and goodness, cherish higher ideals, and strive to do what is right, the Adjuster’s leading grows ever clearer. We need not be discouraged even on days when our feelings run dry. On such days, too, we can choose lofty thoughts, and in that choosing God quietly works.

Today, let us measure our faith not by the temperature of our emotions but by the direction of our thoughts. Quietly ask yourself: What am I thinking right now? Does this thought lead me toward God, or away from him? Then consciously take hold of one noble thought: a thought of understanding someone, of living honestly, of doing the Father’s will. In that place of thought we meet the indwelling spirit. Emotion may follow after as a gift, but it is not the guide. Those who keep their thoughts lifted high are not shaken even in seasons when feelings run dry; quietly but steadily they move toward the Father.
d197.pr: Regardless of your mood, choose one noble thought for today and bring it to mind again and again.
